title: The Digital Canvas
text:
Before painting with light, we must understand our canvas.


Screens comprise millions of tiny squares called Pixels (Picture Elements). Each pixel is not a single colour but a blend of three primary lights: Red, Green, and Blue (RGB).






NoteDeep Dive: Additive Colour





Unlike mixing paint (where red + blue = purple), mixing light is additive. * Red + Green = Yellow * Red + Blue = Magenta * Green + Blue = Cyan * Red + Green + Blue = White






In mathematics, graphs typically place \((0,0)\) in the centre with \(Y\) increasing upwards. Computer graphics differ:

The Origin \((0,0)\) sits at the Top-Left corner.
X increases to the Right.
Y increases Downwards.


Plot.plot({
  grid: true,
  x: {axis: "top", label: "X Axis →"},
  y: {axis: "left", label: "↓ Y Axis"},
  domain: [0, 10],
  marks: [
    Plot.frame(),
    Plot.text([{x: 1, y: 1}], {text: "(1, 1)", x: "x", y: "y", dx: 15, dy: 15}),
    Plot.dot([{x: 1, y: 1}], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "red", r: 5}),
    Plot.text([{x: 5, y: 5}], {text: "(5, 5)", x: "x", y: "y", dx: 15, dy: 15}),
    Plot.dot([{x: 5, y: 5}], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "blue", r: 5})
  ]
})









We access this grid via the HTML5 Canvas API using the <canvas> element.
<!-- MAIN RENDERING SURFACE -->
<canvas id="canvas" tabindex="0"></canvas>
In src/engine.js, we establish a connection to this element to draw upon it.
// Canvas Context configuration
const canvas = document.getElementById('canvas');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', {
  alpha: false,
  willReadFrequently: true,
});
The context (ctx) is our tool for modifying the canvas.






TipPerformance: Resizing



Resizing the browser window is computationally expensive. Our engine employs a debounce function to ensure the grid is only recalculated once the user stops adjusting the window, preventing the simulation from freezing.

Memory & Data
text:
Simulating reality requires storing vast amounts of information. Every pixel must know its colour, light velocity, and whether it represents a wall or empty air.


We call the sum of this information the State. In our engine, state resides in RAM (Random Access Memory).



The most efficient way to store a list in a computer is an Array. Picture an array as a long shelf where every item has a specific number (an index).



Programmers might typically create an Object for every pixel:
// Array of Structures (AoS) - SLOW
let pixel = { red: 1.0, green: 0.5, velocityX: 0.1 };
However, managing 200,000 objects is slow. Every time the computer seeks a new object, it may look in a completely different memory location. This is a Cache Miss, a primary cause of software sluggishness.
Instead, we use a single massive array of numbers and use Offsets to locate data. This Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout keeps related data tightly packed, which the CPU prefers.






NoteAnalogy: The Library Shelf





Imagine a library. * AoS: Books are organised by Author. To find all red books, you must check every aisle. * SoA: Books are organised by Colour. All red books sit on one shelf, allowing you to grab them instantly.



In src/engine.js, we define these “shelves” using the FIELD constant.
/**
 * Memory layout offsets.
 * Access a pixel's property by: index = (y * width + x) * STRIDE + OFFSET.
 */
const FIELD = {
  R: 0,
  G: 1,
  B: 2, // Spectral Energy (Colour)
  VEL_X: 4,
  VEL_Y: 5, // Momentum Vector (Flow direction)
  DEPTH: 7, // Distance from camera (Topology)
};

const STRIDE = 14; // Total slots per pixel
We allocate one giant block of memory for the entire universe:
State.lattice = new Float32Array(TOTAL_PIXELS * STRIDE);
Float32Array is a TypedArray that stores only decimal numbers. It is extremely fast.

MathLib

.nextFloat() ⇒ number
.toHyperbolic(x, y, z) ⇒ Array.<number>
.aces(x) ⇒ number





Fast pseudo-random number generator using Linear Congruential Generator (LCG). Provides deterministic random values based on internal seed state. Uses the same parameters as the POSIX rand48 family.
Kind: static method of MathLib
Returns: number - Pseudo-random float in range [0, 1)
Algorithm: LCG formula: seed = (a × seed + c) mod m Where: a = 1664525, c = 1013904223, m = 2³² Output: seed / 2³² to normalise to [0, 1)
Performance: O(1) - Single multiply-add operation
Deterministic: true - Same seed produces same sequence
Example
// Generate random positions
const x = MathLib.nextFloat() * width;
const y = MathLib.nextFloat() * height;




Poincaré Ball Projection. Compresses infinite Euclidean distance into a 0.0-1.0 range.
Kind: static method of MathLib
Returns: Array.<number> - [x, y, z] projected coordinates.



Param
Type

number

number

ACES (Academy Colour Encoding System) tone mapping curve. Maps High Dynamic Range (HDR) values to Low Dynamic Range (LDR) for display on standard monitors. Preserves colour relationships and provides smooth highlight rolloff.
Kind: static method of MathLib
Returns: number - Tone-mapped LDR value (typically [0, 1])
Algorithm: Rational function approximation: f(x) = (x(ax + b)) / (x(cx + d) + e) Constants tuned for perceptually pleasing results
See: https://knarkowicz.wordpress.com/2016/01/06/aces-filmic-tone-mapping-curve/

Example
// Tone map HDR pixel values
const hdrColour = 5.2;  // Bright light source
const ldrColour = MathLib.aces(hdrColour);  // ~0.95

Performs ray-sphere intersection using geometric algebra. Uses the discriminant method to solve the quadratic equation formed by substituting the ray equation into the sphere equation.
Kind: static method of Scene
Returns: Object - Intersection result
Algorithm: Solves: |P(t) - C|² = r² Where: P(t) = O + tD (ray equation) Expands to: at² + bt + c = 0 Discriminant: Δ = b² - 4ac If Δ > 0: two intersections (entry and exit) Takes nearest positive t value

Type
Description

Array.<number>
Ray direction [x, y, z], should be normalised



Properties








Name
Type
Description

number
Distance along ray to intersection (1e9 if no hit)


obj
Object | null
The sphere object that was hit, or null



Example
const ray = {origin: [0, 0, -5], direction: [0, 0, 1]};
const hit = Scene.trace(ray.origin, ray.direction);
if (hit.obj) {
  console.log(`Hit sphere at distance ${hit.t}`);
}

Example
const hit = Scene.trace(ro, rd);
const shading = Scene.shade(hit, ro, rd);

  // Use shading.albedo, shading.emission, etc.
  const finalColour = shading.albedo.map((c, i) => 
    c * shading.diffuse * shading.falloff + shading.emission[i]
  );
}

  const finalColour = shading.albedo.map((c, i) => 
    c * shading.diffuse * shading.falloff + shading.emission[i]
  );
}

title: Performance Benchmarking
text:
This page allows you to evaluate how the Hybrid Fluid-Light Transport engine performs on your specific hardware.


The simulation below runs a standardised “Stress Test” to measure the limits of the Cellular Automata (CA) and Ray Tracing stages.





Treatment of light as a fluid is computationally demanding. Unlike standard GPU-based shaders, our engine currently runs entirely on the CPU within the JavaScript main thread.







graph TD
    A[Input Handling] --> B[Ray Tracing]
    B --> C[Advection Stage]
    C --> D[Diffusion Stage]
    D --> E[Rendering Stage]
    
    style B fill:#f9f,stroke:#333
    style C fill:#bbf,stroke:#333
    style D fill:#bbf,stroke:#333







Ray Tracing: Calculates where light enters the system. Scaling is \(O(\text{Ray Count} \times \text{Resolution})\).
Fluid Stages: Moves energy across the grid. Scaling is \(O(\text{Grid Width} \times \text{Grid Height})\).





Adjust the parameters below to see their theoretical impact on your frame budget (16.6ms for 60 FPS).

viewof res = Inputs.select([
  {label: "Low (160x90)", value: 14400},
  {label: "Medium (320x180)", value: 57600},
  {label: "High (640x360)", value: 230400}
], {label: "Grid Resolution"})

viewof rays = Inputs.range([8, 128], {value: 64, step: 8, label: "Rays per Frame"})

msPerPixel = 0.00007 // Estimated CPU time per pixel advection/diffusion
msPerRay = 0.05      // Estimated CPU time per ray cast

totalTime = (res * msPerPixel) + (rays * msPerRay)
fps = Math.min(60, 1000 / totalTime)

md`
### Predicted Frame Time: **${totalTime.toFixed(2)}ms**
### Predicted FPS: **${fps.toFixed(1)}**

${totalTime > 16.6 ? 
    "⚠️ **Performance Warning**: This configuration exceeds the 16.6ms budget. Expect stuttering." : 
    "✅ **Optimal**: This should run smoothly at 60 FPS."}
`





















































To improve performance in future versions, we are exploring:

Web Workers: Moving the Diffusion and Advection loops to background threads.
SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data): Using Float32Array with vectorized operations via WebAssembly.
GPU Acceleration: Ports of the CA logic to WebGL/WebGPU compute shaders.

title: Fluid Light Transport Engine
text:
A hybrid Ray-Tracing and Cellular Automata rendering engine.
This project explores a novel approach to real-time global illumination by treating light as a fluid substance. It combines the geometric precision of stochastic ray tracing with the organic flow of fluid dynamics algorithms.






NoteLaunch Scene



Click here to open the interactive scene in a dedicated view.




The engine pipeline consists of two distinct phases: Injection (Ray Tracing) and Propagation (Fluid Dynamics).





graph TD
    A[Scene Data] -->|Inject| B[Ray Tracing Phase]
    B -->|Photons| C[Screen-Space Grid]
    C -->|Advection| D[Fluid Solver Phase]
    D -->|Flow| E[Cellular Automata]
    E -->|Render| F[Final Composite]
    
    style A fill:#f9f,stroke:#333
    style B fill:#bbf,stroke:#333
    style D fill:#bfb,stroke:#333
    style F fill:#f96,stroke:#333


 Fluid Light Transport Pipeline 








We use stochastic ray tracing to probe the scene geometry. Instead of fully resolving the path, rays simply “inject” energy (light) into the screen-space grid at the first hit point.



Once light is in the grid, it behaves like a fluid. * Advection: Light carried by its momentum (direction). * Diffusion: Light spreading into neighbouring pixels (soft shadows).



To prevent light bleeding between disconnected objects (e.g., a foreground sphere and a background wall), we check the Depth Buffer. If the depth difference between pixels is too large, the “fluid” considers it a wall and bounces off.

title: Preface
text:
This document provides a Guided Technical Walkthrough of the Hybrid Fluid-Light Transport engine.
Rather than focusing on jargon, we explore the underlying architecture. We build our understanding from the first principles of digital rasterisation to the complex simulation of non-linear light transport.








TipInteractive Demo



Experience the engine in real-time! Move your mouse to control the light source. Notice the soft shadows, colour bleeding, and ambient occlusion computed entirely through fluid simulation.
Open Full Screen Visualisation →










NoteDemo Troubleshooting



If the screen remains black, ensure you are viewing this through a web server (like quarto preview or GitHub Pages). The engine requires fetch() to load scene data, which is often blocked on local file:// access.





WASD: Move camera
Arrow Keys: Look around
Left Click + Drag: Rotate view
Right Click: Move light source
Space: Cycle visualisation modes





In real-time computer graphics, we typically face a choice:

Ray Tracing: Offers extreme precision (like real-world light) but is computationally expensive, especially for soft, diffuse effects.
Rasterisation: The standard for games; it is incredibly fast but struggles with complex “global illumination” (how light bounces around).

This book explores a “third way”: Hybrid Fluid-Light Transport. We treat light not merely as rays, but as a fluid substance that flows across the scene. This yields beautiful, organic lighting at a fraction of the cost.



We aim to demystify the following code:
/**
 * @fileoverview Hybrid Fluid-Light Transport Engine.
 * This technique creates soft shadows, colour bleeding, and ambient occlusion
 * purely through 2D pixel-neighbour interactions.
 */
By the end of this book, you will understand exactly what that means and how to implement it.



This book offers two complementary paths through the material:

Conceptual JourneyQuick Reference


Learn the architecture and algorithms from first principles:
Foundation (Chapters 1-3) 1. The Digital Canvas — Understanding the screen as a programmable grid 2. The Logic — JavaScript fundamentals for interactive graphics 3. The Memory — Efficient data structures for real-time simulation
Core Algorithms (Chapters 4-7) 4. The Mathematics — Vector operations and spatial reasoning 5. Ray Tracing — Geometric intersection and light injection 6. Fluid Simulation — Cellular automata for light propagation 7. The Main Loop — Orchestrating the complete system
Reference (Chapters 8-9) 8. Troubleshooting — Common issues and solutions 9. API Reference — Complete 1:1 code documentation


Browse by topic or problem:

Getting Started: Chapter 1: Canvas
Understanding Vectors: Chapter 4: Math
Ray Tracing Basics: Chapter 5: Raytracing
Fluid Mechanics: Chapter 6: Fluids
Performance Issues: Chapter 8: Troubleshooting
Complete API: Chapter 9: API Reference










NoteDocumentation Sync



The API reference is automatically regenerated from JSDoc comments in src/engine.js on every build, ensuring perfect synchronisation with the source code.





The Hybrid Fluid-Light Transport engine is under active development. Planned features include:

Refraction Support: Bending light as it passes through different “fluid” densities.
Spectrum Simulation: Splitting light into RGB wavelengths for chromatic aberration.
WebWorker Offloading: Moving the heavy CA computation to a background thread to improve frame rates.

title: Simulating Fluids
Simulating Fluids
text:
Light Intensity \(\approx\) Fluid Pressure (Quantity)
Light Direction \(\approx\) Fluid Velocity (Flow direction)

This analogy allows us to use fluid dynamics algorithms to simulate light transport through 2D space.

title: Simulating Fluids
Simulating Fluids
Simulating Fluids
Simulating Fluids
The Maths of Space
text:
To simulate light, we must describe location and movement using Vectors.


A Vector is simply an arrow with: 1. Origin: Where it starts. 2. Direction: Which way it points. 3. Magnitude: How long it is.
In our 2D grid, a vector is often just two numbers: \((x, y)\).

\((1, 0)\) points Right.
\((0, 1)\) points Down.
\((-1, 0)\) points Left.







TipAPI Reference



See the complete vector implementation in API Reference → Vec2.




Sometimes we care only about direction, not length. If we shrink a vector so its length is exactly \(1.0\), we call it a Unit Vector or say it is Normalised.
Normalising a vector is like noting the direction a finger points, whilst ignoring the finger’s length.

viewof vectorX = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "X"})
viewof vectorY = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Y"})

length = Math.sqrt(vectorX * vectorX + vectorY * vectorY)
normalizedX = length > 0 ? vectorX / length : 0
normalizedY = length > 0 ? vectorY / length : 0

Plot.plot({
  grid: true,
  x: {domain: [-2, 2]},
  y: {domain: [-2, 2]},
  marks: [
    Plot.frame(),
    Plot.arrow([{x1: 0, y1: 0, x2: vectorX, y2: vectorY}], {x1: "x1", y1: "y1", x2: "x2", y2: "y2", stroke: "red", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.arrow([{x1: 0, y1: 0, x2: normalizedX, y2: normalizedY}], {x1: "x1", y1: "y1", x2: "x2", y2: "y2", stroke: "blue", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.text([{x: vectorX, y: vectorY, label: `Original (${vectorX.toFixed(2)}, ${vectorY.toFixed(2)})`}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", dy: -10, fill: "red"}),
    Plot.text([{x: normalizedX, y: normalizedY, label: `Normalised (${normalizedX.toFixed(2)}, ${normalizedY.toFixed(2)})`}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", dy: 15, fill: "blue"})
  ]
})











































Red arrow: Original vector with length \(= {length.toFixed(3)}\)
Blue arrow (dashed): Normalised version with length \(= 1.0\)




To determine the distance of a light source, we use the Pythagorean Theorem:
\[ a^2 + b^2 = c^2 \]
Or in code:
const dist = Math.sqrt(x*x + y*y);
We use this in Scene.shade to calculate light fall-off over distance (Inverse Square Law).



Our engine uses vectors extensively for:

Position: Where objects are in 2D space
Velocity: How fast and in which direction light flows
Direction: Ray casting and collision detection






graph LR
    A[Light Source<br/>Position: 5,3] -->|Cast Ray<br/>Direction: 1,0| B[Pixel Grid]
    B -->|Hit Detection<br/>Distance: √((x₂-x₁)²+(y₂-y₁)²)| C[Sphere]
    C -->|Reflect<br/>New Direction| D[Secondary Ray]












NoteImplementation Details




Vector addition: Combines positions or velocities (API Reference)
Dot product: Measures alignment between directions
Normalisation: Used in ray direction calculations

title: The Main Loop
The Main Loop
text:
Animation is an illusion. By updating the screen 60 times per second (60 Hz), we trick the eye into seeing motion.
JavaScript provides requestAnimationFrame. This instructs the browser: “When ready to paint the screen, call my function first.”
Why not setInterval? Because requestAnimationFrame pauses when you switch tabs, saving battery!

title: The Main Loop
text:

title: The Main Loop
The Main Loop
text:
We have journeyed from the humble pixel to a complex, hybrid fluid-light transport simulation.
By treating light as a fluid, we create beautiful, organic lighting effects that respond to the environment in real-time. We optimised this by understanding computer memory (SoA) and employing simplified physics (Cellular Automata) rather than calculating every single photon perfectly.
Furthermore, our engine now monitors Grid Sparsity—the ratio of active light regions to empty space. This telemetry allows us to gauge efficiency and ensure we only process pixels that truly matter.
This is the power of the Hybrid Fluid-Light Transport Engine.

title: Casting Rays
Casting Rays
text:
In reality, light travels from a bulb to your eye. In computer graphics, we work in reverse. We shoot a ray from the “Camera” (your eye) through every screen pixel to see what it strikes.





flowchart LR
    A[Eye/Camera] -->|1. Cast Ray| B[Screen Pixel]
    B -->|2. Trace Through Scene| C{Hit Object?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Calculate Colour<br/>& Lighting]
    C -->|No| E[Return Background<br/>Colour]
    D --> F[Display Result]
    E --> F


 Ray tracing flow: from eye through screen to scene 









TipWhy Reverse?



Forward ray tracing (light → eye) is inefficient because most rays miss the camera. Reverse tracing (eye → scene) ensures every ray contributes to the image.

title: Casting Rays
Casting Rays
text:
Our scene comprises spheres. To check if a ray hits a sphere, we use algebra. A sphere is defined as all points at a distance \(r\) from a centre point \(C\).


A sphere centred at \(\mathbf{C}\) with radius \(r\) satisfies:
\[ |\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{C}|^2 = r^2 \]
Substituting the ray equation \(\mathbf{P}(t) = \mathbf{O} + t\mathbf{D}\):
\[ |\mathbf{O} + t\mathbf{D} - \mathbf{C}|^2 = r^2 \]
This becomes a quadratic equation:
\[ at^2 + bt + c = 0 \]
Where: - \(a = \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{D}\) (usually 1 if direction is normalised) - \(b = 2\mathbf{D} \cdot (\mathbf{O} - \mathbf{C})\) - \(c = |\mathbf{O} - \mathbf{C}|^2 - r^2\)
The discriminant \(\Delta = b^2 - 4ac\) determines if we hit:



Discriminant
Result




\(\Delta < 0\)
No intersection (ray misses sphere)


\(\Delta = 0\)
Tangent (ray grazes sphere)


\(\Delta > 0\)
Two intersections (ray enters and exits)






This is implemented in Scene.trace within src/engine.js:
/* src/engine.js */
trace: function(ro, rd) {
    // ...
    const oc = {x: ro.x - sphere.x, y: ro.y - sphere.y};
1    const b = 2 * (rd.x * oc.x + rd.y * oc.y);
2    const c = (oc.x * oc.x + oc.y * oc.y) - r * r;
    
3    const d = b * b - c;
4    if (d > 0) {
5        const t = (-b - Math.sqrt(d)) / 2;
        // We hit the sphere at distance t!
    }
}

1

Calculates coefficient \(b = 2\mathbf{D} \cdot (\mathbf{O} - \mathbf{C})\)

2

Calculates coefficient \(c = |\mathbf{O} - \mathbf{C}|^2 - r^2\)

3

Computes discriminant \(\Delta = b^2 - 4ac\) (simplified since \(a=1\))

4

Positive discriminant means intersection

5

Solves for \(t\) using quadratic formula (takes nearest hit)

title: Casting Rays
text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as Ray Origin
    participant R as Ray
    participant S as Sphere
    participant G as Grid
    
    O->>R: Cast ray with direction
    loop Every step distance t
        R->>S: Check intersection
        alt Hit detected (d > 0)
            S-->>G: Inject light energy
            Note over S,G: Energy = f(distance, angle)
        else No hit
            R->>R: Advance ray (t += step)
        end
    end
